verdict.summary: Oracle's AI demand is real; its funding problem is equally real. Q4 FY2026 revenue rose 21% to $19.2B, OCI climbed 93% to $5.8B and RPO reached $638B. Backlog becomes equity value only after Oracle finances and powers data centers, then collects cloud revenue. FY2026 operating cash flow was $32B, yet free cash flow was negative $23.7B. The $20B common ATM had sold no shares by May 31, leaving all capacity available; a separate $5B 6.50% mandatory convertible can produce roughly 25.0M-31.2M common shares in 2029. The dated valuation is 4.9x FY2027 targeted revenue with a negative 5.4% trailing FCF yield. September 10 earnings veto execution. After review, $153.98 activates risk to $151.91, then $159.2599 and the $181.0899 range projection.
whyAvoid: FY2027 funding is expected near $40B of debt and equity.

business.overview:
Oracle earns recurring support, cloud applications, database subscriptions and infrastructure consumption. The installed database estate anchors renewals and migration, while OCI supplies the fastest growth. RPO captures signed cloud commitments, but recognition depends on delivering capacity over contract terms.

AI demand reaches Oracle through GPU clusters, networking, database access and sovereign cloud regions. OCI revenue rises after campuses obtain power, hardware is installed and customers accept service. Oracle can cross-sell database and applications if utilization earns an adequate return on construction.

The break point is capital intensity. Oracle spent enough in FY2026 to drive free cash flow to negative $23.7B and plans debt plus equity financing for the next build phase. Delayed power, concentrated counterparties, weak utilization or higher funding costs can turn $638B RPO into leverage and dilution before profitable revenue.

Database support cash flow can subsidize part of the build, but it cannot neutralize unlimited construction spending. Investors need campus-level delivery, utilization and financing disclosures to judge whether OCI growth is compounding franchise value or merely enlarging the balance sheet.
business.moat: Oracle's moat combines mission-critical database lock-in, decades of application and support relationships, and deployment across OCI, customer premises and other clouds. That installed base lowers migration friction into OCI. It does not remove hyperscaler competition, construction bottlenecks or the cost of financing AI capacity.

capitalStructure.shareHistory: Oracle had roughly 2.88B common shares outstanding. The February 2 ATM authorized up to $20B of primary common sales, but the May 31 Form 10-K states no shares had been sold, leaving full capacity. Oracle separately issued 100M depositary shares for $5B gross, representing 50,000 Series D mandatory-convertible preferred shares. Conversion on January 15, 2029 implies 24.99M-31.24M common shares, producing a minimum potential denominator of approximately 2.905B-2.911B before stock-paid dividends and employee awards. The exact theoretical fully diluted count remains unavailable; ATM capacity is authorized but not issued equity.

filings.finding: The May 31, 2026 Form 10-K is Oracle's latest periodic filing. It reports $67.4B FY2026 revenue, $32B operating cash flow, negative $23.7B free cash flow, no common shares sold under the $20B ATM through year-end, and the completed $5B mandatory-convertible preferred issuance.

The February-quarter Form 10-Q predates the June annual report and is retained only for interim operating and liquidity context. It is a periodic report, not an ATM sale, primary common issuance, secondary distribution or debt takedown.

The earnings current report and direct Exhibit 99.1 provide the latest growth, margin, KPI and guidance facts. This is operating disclosure, not a shelf, ATM, primary equity sale, secondary offering or debt issuance.

The February 2 424B5 created an at-the-market program for up to $20B of primary Oracle common stock through named sales agents. It authorized capacity rather than proving sales; the May 31 Form 10-K later states zero shares sold and $20B remaining.

The February 3 424B5 added ten sales agents to the existing $20B primary common-stock ATM. It did not increase capacity, report any shares sold or create a separate program; it is neither debt nor a secondary-holder distribution.

The June 23 424B5 superseded the February 3 agent supplement and revised the sales-agent roster for the same $20B primary common ATM. It disclosed no new capacity and no executed share sales, debt issuance or secondary offering.

The February 2 preliminary 424B5 proposed depositary shares representing Series D mandatory-convertible preferred stock, with final size and pricing not yet fixed. It was primary equity-linked financing with prospective common dilution, not straight debt, an ATM or a secondary sale.

The final February 4 424B5 priced 100M depositary shares at $50 each for $5B gross, each representing 1/2,000th of one 6.50% Series D mandatory-convertible preferred share. The 50,000 preferred shares convert January 15, 2029 into about 24.99M-31.24M common shares before dividend adjustments; this was completed primary equity-linked financing.

Credible RPO conversion, bounded FY2027 capex and disclosed ATM usage are required.
